extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, practitioners, judges, and administrative agencies addressing First Amendment issues (especially social media/moderation)
extracted.subtask_short: First Amendment forum and speech analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Doctrinal account of First Amendment standards for classifying forums (traditional, designated/limited, non-public), the government-speech doctrine, and historical/ normative considerations (neo‑Roman liberty) that inform how speech restrictions on government property and agency social media should be evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neo‑Roman negative liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberty as non‑dependence: negative liberty is not merely absence of interference but the absence of dependence on another’s will and the absence of awareness of such dependence, because awareness of tentative rights leads to self‑censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical sources (Roman law, Tacitus, Sallust, Machiavelli, Skinner) show awareness of dependence constrains speech in ways beyond direct coercion; this concept affects how one reconciles individual free speech and republican self‑government and suggests courts should consider dependence (not just interference) when assessing speech environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdependence of individual liberty and democratic self‑government (normative lens)
rubrics_metrics.description: First Amendment doctrine should value both individual liberty (including human dignity/autonomy) and democratic self‑government as ends and means; focusing exclusively on one value at the expense of the other yields impoverished analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doctrine and doctrinal choice (e.g., public forum vs government speech) should weigh how protections for individual speech serve collective self‑governance and vice versa; historical tradition (Founders, Brandeis, Post) supports viewing the values as mutually informing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional public forum test
rubrics_metrics.description: Properties 'traditionally' open for public assembly and discussion (streets, parks, sidewalks) are traditional public fora; content‑based restrictions in such fora are permissible only if they satisfy strict scrutiny, and viewpoint restrictions are forbidden; only limited time/place/manner restrictions may be imposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Hague v. CIO; Grayned; Mosley; strict scrutiny defined as necessary to serve a compelling state interest and narrowly drawn; time/place/manner allowed to prevent incompatible activities (e.g., two parades).

rubrics_metrics.name: Designated public forum standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A designated public forum is public property the State has opened for public expressive use; content‑based prohibitions in a designated forum must meet strict scrutiny (same burdens as traditional public forum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court references: Perry, Cornelius, Pleasant Grove; the Court has rarely (if ever) found a true designated public forum in practice; the concept carries the same rigorous First Amendment protection as traditional fora.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited public forum standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A limited (or limitedly designated) public forum is one the government opens for expressive activity but confines it to certain speakers or subjects; because the forum is limited from the start, strict scrutiny does not apply and the government may impose restrictions tailored to the forum’s limited purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrictions must be reasonable and viewpoint neutral; examples include a public university's student activities fund, public school facilities, and certain libraries (Rosenberger, Good News Club, Widmar, Lamb’s Chapel). Pleasant Grove clarifies distinction between designated and limited fora.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non‑public forum standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Public property that is neither traditionally nor intentionally opened for public discourse is a non‑public forum; the government, as property owner, may regulate access and expression so long as restrictions are reasonable and viewpoint neutral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sidewalk in front of a post office (Kokinda), airport terminals (International Soc. for Krishna Consciousness v. Lee), Combined Federal Campaign (Cornelius), residential mailboxes (USPS v. Council of Greenburgh Civic Ass’ns). A ban on soliciting is a typical reasonable, viewpoint‑neutral restriction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forum classification factors (tradition, government intent, physical characteristics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts classify fora by reference to (1) historical/traditional use of the property for expressive activity, and (2) the government's intent in creating or using the property; Justice Kennedy has urged attention to physical characteristics and actual uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perry emphasizes tradition and intent as guiding stars; Kennedy suggests focusing on 'actual, physical characteristics' to avoid permitting governments to avoid public‑forum status simply by articulating a non‑speech purpose. The choice of factors affects whether stricter scrutiny applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grayned 'basic incompatibility' test (time/place/manner incompatibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: A forum restriction may be upheld if the manner of expression is fundamentally incompatible with the normal activity of a particular place at a particular time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to analyze time/place/manner restrictions (Grayned v. City of Rockford); examples include preventing incompatible uses such as two parades on the same street or speech that interferes with a school’s core functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: General prohibition on viewpoint discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: As a general First Amendment rule, government may not restrict expression because of its message, ideas, subject matter, or content (i.e., viewpoint discrimination is prohibited).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mosley and other precedents articulate this broad principle; however, recognized doctrinal exceptions (government speech, certain funding decisions, institution‑specific roles) may permit selection that appears viewpoint‑discriminatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government speech doctrine (definition and consequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the government itself is the speaker, the Free Speech Clause does not restrict the content of that speech; determining when the government is speaking is legally unsettled and fact‑specific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doctrine is recent/imprecise (Johanns v. Livestock Mktg. Ass’n; progenitors include Arkansas Educational Television Comm’n v. Forbes, NEA v. Finley, U.S. v. American Library Ass’n). The doctrine evolved to handle contexts (patronage, selection, programming) where public forum analysis yields odd results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution‑specific role exception (government as patron/educator/librarian)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain government roles—patron of the arts, librarian, educator, broadcaster—may lawfully involve selection and curation that are not governed by the public‑forum strict scrutiny rules; such institution‑specific rules recognize the government's expressive or programmatic functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include NEA grant decisions, library book selection, and curricular choices; public forum doctrine can be ineffectual for evaluating these institutionally embedded selections, so the Court developed tailored analysis in those contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding/program limits treated as government speech (Rust and related doctrine)
rubrics_metrics.description: When government appropriates funds for particular programs, speech conducted under those programs may be constrained by program limits and treated as government speech rather than unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rust v. Sullivan (1991): prohibition on federally funded doctors discussing abortion in family planning programs was upheld as a program funding limitation; Legal Services Corp. v. Velazquez later clarified nuances about when funding restrictions constitute unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination versus permissible government speech/funding choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical consequence: agency social media classification
rubrics_metrics.description: If a federal agency's social media site is classified as a public forum, content‑based restrictions (including bans on offensive language or hate speech) would be subject to strict scrutiny and likely impermissible; classification thus has decisive effects on permissible moderation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the public forum doctrine would require strict scrutiny of content‑based rules, agencies face exposure if courts treat agency social media as traditional or designated fora; conversely, treating such accounts as government speech permits more restrictive moderation/selection.
